summary:
Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), and the law reaches far beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) documents that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and records police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under it.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Official foreign guidance aimed at LGBT+ visitors is current and blunt. In August 2026 the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice for Nigeria warned LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

Trans-specific violence is documented and the response has produced no charges. In August 2024 the beaten body of 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender TikToker, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend. Police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing', and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation; six months later no suspect had been charged.

Police extortion and violence against perceived-gay people continues in current conditions. In March 2025 Lagos police stopped a 24-year-old man, struck him in the mouth with the butt of a police gun, and freed him only after he paid almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'. People affected by the SSMPA describe it as a weaponised law that creates a climate of hostility.

Visitors who use dating apps face a documented entrapment crime. 'Kito' gangs lure LGBTQ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where they are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing; the community counters with exposure forums, including an alert page run by one administrator that draws 43,000 followers, and with sting operations.

Group arrests at social venues recur across the country: more than 100 party-goers at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018; 57 young men in Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018; the 'Warri 67' in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023; and 76 people arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. Men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held in jail for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by the end of 2011.

Trans expression itself carries exposure. In September 2022 transgender Nigerians reported fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine; she served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison in Lagos and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison would hold 'the crossdresser', reflecting discretionary placement. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

A decade after the SSMPA took effect, reporting in August 2024 concludes that the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse: LGBTQ Nigerians report lost job prospects, and attacks have increased since the law passed.
tangentialFactors:
The legal regime is layered rather than recent. The SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation, so the criminal exposure a visitor encounters predates 2014 and now sits alongside religious criminal penalties in the north, producing two overlapping systems of punishment in one country.

Public opinion constrains protection as much as statute does. A 2015 survey by Bisi Alimi's organisation found that only 30% of Nigerians agree LGBTQ persons should receive education, healthcare and housing, and no political party endorses LGBTQ rights.

The formal constitutional guarantee does not translate into a claimable right. Section 17(3)(d) of the Constitution nominally guarantees adequate medical and health care to all citizens, but there is no enacted legislation protecting against discrimination generally, and the SSMPA is described by those affected as a law that has effectively sanctioned abuse.

Enforcement patterns have been consistent over long periods rather than concentrated in a single purge: arrests in 2007, mass arrests at hotels and parties in 2018, 2023 and the same year's Gombe raid, with detainees held for years awaiting trials that never conclude.

Nigeria's approach is outside the regional norm its neighbours have moved toward in part, and the 2026 foreign-office warning places the country among jurisdictions where a government explicitly advises LGBT travellers of imprisonment and death-penalty risk.
localsOnly:
Nigerian LGBTQ people face documented barriers to healthcare and to reporting crime. Many fear seeking medical care or reporting offences because of the risk of arrest and of 'kito' extortion, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and their allies to abandon community health and education work.

Organised community infrastructure exists under pressure. NGOs Global Rights and The Independent Project provided LGBT groups with HIV/AIDS awareness training, according to the 2011 US State Department report, while the House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008 and some were threatened, beaten and stoned. LGBTQ-friendly venues face closure risk on the same pattern.

The Federal Ministry of Education maintains a national policy on safety, security and violence-free schools in all Nigerian schools that prohibits discrimination explicitly including on 'sexual orientation'. In practice, religious institutions play a crucial role in education, and mainstream interpretations of Islam and Christianity drive stigmatisation of LGBTQ students.

Young people bear a large share of enforcement: 76 people were arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023, on top of the mass hotel arrests of 2018 and the Warri arrests of 2023.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Bobrisky was held in a male or female section at Kirikiri is not recorded in the sourced biography; the press coverage at sentencing indicates the placement was discretionary, and the October 2024 panel addressed only the lawfulness of the security classification, not the sex of the unit.

Whether the 2022 proposals to criminalise cross-dressing have since been enacted as legislation is unresolved in this inventory; the available source reports only that transgender Nigerians feared the proposals at that date.

No hate-crime statute, gender-recognition procedure, or rule governing which marker a trans visitor's passport carries is sourced for Nigeria here. Entry and visa screening conditions for trans travellers, and the treatment of foreign detainees in relation to placement, remain not sourced and would need separate verification.

The ten-year assessment of the SSMPA rests on reporting and community testimony rather than on a quantified national dataset of prosecutions; arrest figures cited come from specific documented raids and do not constitute a national total.
